Cathedral City: A Line Extension Done Right

Cathedral City

Cheese Peelers and Spreadable Cheese

4.8

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market. 

Speak to our innovation team today!

This week’s Innovation Of The Week comes from Cathedral City cheddar and gives us an opportunity to talk line extensions. How do you find a line extension that works, letting you keep the elements that make your brand distinctive and successful while not cannibalising your existing products? 

It’s something Test Your Innovation (TYI) is particularly good at spotting. A TYI Star Rating is based on a combination of individual emotional response and market-oriented ‘wisdom of crowds’ prediction via a “share-buying game”. That makes it sensitive to line extension concepts that people instinctively recognise as too weird or too similar to the parent brand. 

Cathedral City, on the other hand, are building on what they’re best known for – strong, tasty cheddar cheese – and finding new ways to deliver it. The concept we’re looking at is for a pair of new Cathedral City formats: a cheese string “peeler” and a pot of spreadable Cathedral City. 

These are products consumers will already be familiar with from other cheese brands – spreadable cheese portions and cheese strings have been staples of children’s lunch boxes for decades. But it’s also true that the existing options can be rather bland and tasteless – far away from the rich real cheese flavour Cathedral City brings. 

From the Test Your Innovation diagnostics, we can see how real consumers latch on to these ideas. The new products are seen as especially appealing to children in the “Predicted Target” chart – though importantly they’re not exclusively for kids, people predict above average appeal for adults too. Meanwhile the comments specifically call out the flavour as the reason these new ideas are an improvement on existing cheese snacks: “Wonderful spreadable cheese with more flavour” and “Like a cheesestring with real cheese” are two of the Advantages people found. 

Looking at the Implicit Attributes chart, where people quickly indicate whether the new idea matches each adjective, it’s clear that Cathedral City’s existing brand equity is the biggest asset here. The new product gets only average scores on “innovative” and “unique” but way over the norm on “Trustworthy”, “High Quality” and “Recognisable”. 

In other words, this is a type of product people already know but brought to them by a brand they trust and see as higher quality than the current options. You couldn’t ask for a sweeter line extension spot. 

And the overall metrics bear that out – this is a very strong 4.8-Star innovation. It does particularly well on emotional response and on the share trading game (with 69% of people saying they’d buy shares in the idea). It’s an example of a line extension done right – extending a quality the brand is known for (taste and flavour) into areas where people are looking for those options. Testing reveals that.

Boots Keeps It Positive With an Autumn Winner

Boots

Give It Some Boots

4.4

Make creative your competitive edge; unlock insights and inspiration from 100,000+ ads, rooted in emotional response, to predict and improve your creative’s business impact. Access every Ad Of The Week in our Topical Ads categories.

Boots and agency VML are going big and bold for Autumn with a major new brand campaign, built around the tagline “Give It Some Boots”. Like many of the retailer’s recent successful campaigns it’s an upbeat, lively, emotional ad built around the brand’s keen understanding of consumer needs. It launched in Autumn which is a key moment for people to reset, refresh and grab hold of life, looking tough times and difficulties in the face with new positivity. 

That’s the vibe of the “Give It Some Boots” 60 second hero ad, which earns our Ad Of The Week spot this week. Soundtracked by a sharp new reworking of classic tune “These Boots Are Made For Walking”, the ad is a montage of women of all ages, looks and walks of life as they tackle their beauty dilemmas head-on (with a little help from Boots, of course).  

There’s dancing, smiles and plenty of sympathy as people from a young person with skin troubles to a woman dealing with chemo-induced hair loss find the products and advice they’re looking for. It’s an ad that doesn’t flinch from life’s tough realities, but which also encourages viewers to take them on and ‘give it some Boots’. 

How well has the brand judged consumers’ mood? Extremely well, if our Test Your Ad results are any guide. “Give It Some Boots” is a really strong performer on both our short- and long-term measures, in the top 10% of the general retail category for both, which is exactly what you’d hope from a campaign intended to work as a brand-building platform. 

On the headline Star Rating, which predicts the potential for long-term business growth and effects, “Give It Some Boots” gets a strong 4.4-Star Rating, which puts it in the top 6% of general retail ads. Retail categories tend to be dominated by high-scoring Christmas ads, so for a new brand-building campaign, launched in Autumn, to be performing at this level is a really excellent result for Boots. 

The ad is equally strong on Spike Rating, which predicts short-term sales boosts. The high energy and strong branding means it gets an Exceptional Spike score, in the top 7% for the category. The ad’s early branding is particularly effective – it has an exceptional Fast Fluency score, with 84% of viewers recognising it as a Boots ad within the opening few seconds. 

With Test Your Ad Pro we can drill down to find out what’s driving the positive response – it’s a good, all-round ad with “amused” and “uplifted” particularly powerful Types Of Happiness. Positive verbatim comments note the inclusive casting, the dancing and a general warmth towards the brand (which the ad will only help reinforce). 

That inclusivity might be why it resonates especially well with younger viewers – our demographic breakdown is only indicative, as the sample sizes are small, but it shows that both men and women rate the ad as 4-Stars but that the younger (18-34) audience go all the way to 5-Stars. With younger viewers being typically harder to reach it’s a sign that Boots’ mix of optimism, realism and vibrant imagination is striking exactly the right note this Autumn.

entry.content:
Tom Ewing
Editor in chief

Published: 26 October 2026

System1 & Advertising Association’s October Ads of the Month

Successful sustainability messaging isn’t just about the message. How it’s delivered is just as important – often more important. This month’s line-up of good ads use different strategies to put a message across: making it personal, stressing the optimistic, and using metaphor. All three of them are great ways a brand with a sustainability message can stand out and win over an audience.

Etsy – “Firsts: Nicky”

We’ll start with Etsy, and a 15-second ad in their campaign spotlighting their individual sellers. In this case it’s Nicky, a ceramicist and painter who makes decorative pieces. The ad shows a quick montage of some of the special moments in other people’s lives that Nicky’s art has decorated, from weddings to christenings to moving in. “I have the best job in the world” says Nicky as the ad ends.

The ad scores 4.0-Stars on Test Your Ad, putting it into the top 10% of all retail ads. It also gets an exceptional 95% Brand Fluency, so people come away from the ad knowing exactly who it’s for. The secret to its success is combining strong branding at the beginning and end with a personal focus.

Rather than talk about the brand in general or what it can do for sellers, Etsy’s ad just shows us one person and the lives she and Etsy helped make more magical. That personal focus is a fantastic tool for sustainability measures too – showing the impact of behaviour change or initiatives on one person or business can be a lot more vivid and meaningful than talking in the abstract.

Guide Dogs – “Unleashed”

Next up it’s an ad for Guide Dogs. The charity sector is an unusual one for advertising, with a lot of similarities and crossover to sustainability-focused organisations. Both have to find ways of talking about sometimes difficult or unpalatable topics without alienating viewers. This ad focuses on “life-changing firsts” that Guide Dogs can provide for people with sight loss, from a child’s first steps to enabling first meetings and first-time activities.

The Test Your Ad ratings tell you how successful the ad is but also how unusual the charity sector is for ads. The ad gets an exceptional Spike Rating – our predictor of short-term impact – but that’s still only a little above the Charity average. The 5.4-Star long term Star Rating though is hugely above the sector norm, in the top 1% of charity ads. In other words, the typical charity ad does a great job at motivating people in the short term but sacrifices long-term brand building. Guide Dogs show that you can do both.

The reason this ad works better is that its outlook is so optimistic. Rather than focusing on the problems a person with sight loss faces, Guide Dogs emphasise the solutions and the opportunities they bring. Their tagline “Life Unleashed” sums that up. For a sustainability-focused brand the lesson is clear – emphasise positive outcomes and you encourage long-term effectiveness as the steps people need to take becomes easier.

BT – “Protecting Brilliant Things”

Finally, there’s a lovely ad from BT which not only spotlights actual sustainable behaviour – a group of beekeepers who work hard to protect their bees from invasive pests – but uses it as a metaphor. Broadband providers do not generally score well on Test Your Ad, as most do not bother with an emotional route, so BT’s 3.3-Star Rating isn’t just good, it’s in the top 12% of all the ads in its category.

The way it achieves this is simple – it uses the beekeepers as a metaphor for the protection BT gives its broadband customers from the invasive internet threats of malware, viruses and fraud. The metaphor makes for a more visually interesting ad but also one that engages the viewer’s mind better than a simple feature-focused ad would. Metaphor is a powerful tool for sustainability themed ads because a lot of sustainability issues seem big or complex, and a metaphor can help bring them back to human scale so they’re less daunting.

Whether it’s taking the personal touch, focusing on the positive, or using metaphor to make behaviour more real, how you say something is often more important than what you’re saying. In our The Greenprint study there are dozens more examples and strategies like this for sustainability messages that can actually work.

Create with Confidence®

Great advertising changes how people feel before it changes what they do.

Testing with real people helps you understand whether your creative is overcoming indifference, building emotional connection, and making your brand impossible to ignore. It shows whether you’re creating work that resonates instinctively, communicates clearly, and earns its place in memory.

Because effectiveness isn’t a matter of opinion. It’s measurable.

With System1’s creative testing solutions, you can optimise every campaign before launch, creating advertising that is more emotional, more distinctive, and more likely to drive long-term commercial growth.

A Headless Hit: Butterfinger’s Horseman Returns for 2026

Butterfinger

Headless Horseman Halloween

4.7

Make creative your competitive edge; unlock insights and inspiration from 100,000+ ads, rooted in emotional response, to predict and improve your creative’s business impact. Access every Ad Of The Week in our Topical Ads categories.

Request a Demo of Test Your Ad Competitive Edge

Halloween ads continue to roll out and as ever it’s the Candy & Gum category which is seeing the most attention and the best new commercials. Candy & Gum is an unusual category whose advertisers face a different problem than many brands. In many sectors, boring category conventions drag the average Test Your Ad score down, and the struggle is to find a way of showcasing your brand in an entertaining manner. 

Candy has the opposite problem. It boasts one of the highest average Test Your Ad Star Ratings, with a norm of 3.9-Stars. Candy is a product with happiness built in, which means a brand has to find ways to stand out against competitors. Halloween is a particular battleground but also the perfect opportunity – there’s a wealth of Halloween imagery allowing a brand to try something different. 

Which brings us to Butterfinger and their excellent Halloween ad, borrowing the classic imagery of the Headless Horseman of Sleepy Hollow. The Horseman – speaking through a carved pumpkin, has stolen some Butterfinger candies. Our 18th century heroes are holding his head hostage for their return. It’s a standoff – until the Horseman falls off his horse and the candies are returned. Tagline: “No-one lays a finger on your Butterfinger this Halloween”. 

The ad first aired last year and was clearly successful enough to earn a return of engagement, meaning Butterfinger’s investment goes further, and consistency and familiarity increases. You can see that familiarity at work in the 99% Brand Fluency rating, which puts Butterfinger in the top 3% of this hard-fought category. 

High Brand Fluency also helps Spike Rating, our predictor of short-term sales boosts, which is vital for a seasonal promotion. The Headless Horseman ad gets exceptional Spike, in the top 6% of the category, showing Butterfinger have themselves a sales powerhouse. No surprise, it was renewed for a second year. The long-term, brand building Star Rating is also in the top 25% of Candy & Gum ads, at 4.7-Stars. 

For a 15-second ad, those are impressive figures. The secrets to Butterfinger’s success here are humor, storytelling, and of course the attention-grabbing cultural reference of the Horseman himself. The ad packs entertaining images (a pumpkin munching a candy bar) and a satisfying reversal (the Horseman falling off his horse) into a very brief runtime. Those elements of showmanship help the ad stand out in a competitive category at a time of year when screens are clogged with candy products. 

When we wrote about the M&Ms x Snickers ad recently, we pointed out that Christmas has perennial ads which are shown every year and become part of the season, but Halloween doesn’t. With brands reusing their most successful Spooky Season inventory, that might be on the verge of changing. The Horseman and Butterfinger could ride out for many more years to come.

Toblerone x Biscoff: A Great Product, A Great Launch

Toblerone

Toblerone x Lotus Biscoff

5.7

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market. 

Speak to our innovation team today!

When you have a great innovation, how do you launch it most effectively? One of the ways Test Your Innovation is so useful for brands is that it goes beyond just identifying the best new ideas and product options. It also includes diagnostics that can help you craft your launch marketing so it has the highest possible impact.

So this week we’re looking at a 5-Star innovation from Toblerone and Lotus Biscoff which also launched with a 5-Star ad, and exploring how some of the diagnostics in the innovation report are visible in the ad too.

Lotus Biscoff are a brand with an established strategy of brand extensions and collaborations – it’s how they’ve grown from a local biscuit brand to an internationally recognised name with a signature flavour. For this innovation they’re partnering with Toblerone, and it’s an excellent fit: two brands with a premium reputation and strong local European heritage. The partnership is not on a new Toblerone bar but instead on ‘Diamond Truffles’ – Toblerone chocolate with a Biscoff flavoured filling in a diamond shape evoking the signature Toblerone triangle.

It’s positioned as a high-class product suitable as an indulgence or a gift, and the Test Your Innovation report shows the Diamond Truffles are extremely popular with the public. They score an exceptional 5.7-Star Rating, close to the maximum possible. They also perform exceptionally on the Emotional Response measure. And they get strong results on the two other parts of the Test Your Innovation package – the share trading game (71% say they would buy shares) and the time spent reaching that decision, which tells us how easy the idea is to ‘get’.

So the headline scores show that this is a really excellent, strong launch in good time for the holiday season. But Test Your Innovation goes deeper, with diagnostics exploring the key attributes people associate with the idea, and the predicted demographics the truffles would appeal to.

What those diagnostics tell us is that the truffles are seen as a sophisticated and smart choice – scoring well above the norm on “High Quality” and “Recommended” but also “Good Value”, a premium-level candy that won’t bust your budget. People also see the Diamond Truffles as having strong adult appeal – they aren’t a chocolate for kids.

Bear those findings in mind when we look at the Test Your Ad results, where Diamond Truffles gets a 5.6-Star Rating, putting it in the top 10% of the highly competitive Candy & Gum category. The ad shows a glamorous woman at an exclusive party in a top hotel, wearing a Diamond Truffle as a pendant around her neck. The lights flicker, and then we see a man has taken the truffle from around her neck and is eating it: an entertaining twist on the idea of a high class jewel thief.

So we know from Test Your Innovation that people would see the ad as having strong orientation with the product – the ad is giving “high-class” and “adult” in exactly the way the TYI voters predicted would appeal. Even the best product needs the right marketing, but understanding public perceptions can help craft that marketing and give your 5-Star Innovation the launch it deserves.

McVitie’s Autumn Ad Is a Slam Dunk

McVitie's

There's Only One That Brings Us All Together. McVitie's.

5.4

Make creative your competitive edge; unlock insights and inspiration from 100,000+ ads, rooted in emotional response, to predict and improve your creative’s business impact. Access every Ad Of The Week in our Topical Ads categories.

Request a Demo of Test Your Ad Competitive Edge

McVitie’s biscuits have been at the heart of British life for almost 200 years. From a morning cuppa with a Rich Tea through to an elevenses Hobnob or teatime Chocolate Digestive, McVitie’s is a snack that’s known and loved across generations. And now, with help from adam&eve/TBWA, the brand is letting us know how proud it is of that. 

“There’s only one that brings us all together” is McVitie’s masterbrand campaign for this autumn, building on their successful ad with Trevor McDonald from 2023, “There’s only one”. That work was about reminding people about McVitie’s powerful heritage status as “the original”, and it scored a very strong 4.5-Stars on Test Your Ad, well above the Bakery Products UK average of 3.7-Stars. 

But the new ad goes one better, landing a  5.4-Star rating for McVitie’s, putting it in the top 5% of all Bakery Products ads. It is McVitie’s best result for a Masterbrand ad.  The Star Rating predicts exceptional potential for long-term share gain and business impact, but the spot also gets an exceptional Spike Rating predicting short-term sales boosts. 

What makes this ad such a success? Rather than rely on a particular celebrity or a long story narrative, McVitie’s go all out here to build an emotional platform that illustrates how the brand fits into the everyday lives of its customers. Right from the opening shot, which takes us to a prenatal yoga class where one pregnant woman sympathetically rolls a pack of biscuits to another, we’re in the middle of real, relatable lives. This ad is all about ordinary people finding humour in their shared rituals – like a biscuit breaking mid-dunk – brought to life on screen in a charming and entertaining way. 

That means it has plenty of one of the most valuable creative elements we see in advertising – what Orlando Wood calls between-ness, the sense of human connection and togetherness expressed not just in dialogue but in glances, gestures and non-verbal communication. Like saying it with McVitie’s biscuits, for instance. The ad creates emotion via this sense of between-ness, which also brings to life McVitie’s brand promise as a social connector – something that brings people together in small but very meaningful ways. 

The excellent Test Your Ad results for this new ad suggest that McVitie’s big autumn campaign will be a huge success. As we head into the colder months consumers will be reminded of the role McVitie’s plays in bringing people together.

entry.content:
Renata Buess
Creative & Media Partnership Director, LATAM (renata.buess@system1research.com)

Published: 15 October 2026

Não é só com fofura que se chega a 4,3 Estrelas.

Ipanema

Você não é todo mundo.

4.3
View in English

“Você não é todo mundo”: a frase que encerra discussões agora vende…sandálias

Existe uma frase que encerra negociações com crianças em qualquer lugar do mundo, sem recurso nem réplica. Costuma ser dita um segundo antes de a criança perceber que o assunto acabou: “Você não é todo mundo.”

Agora imagine essa frase vindo de uma criança. No novo filme de Ipanema, quem diz isso são os pequenos. E quem leva a “bronca” são os adultos.

O anúncio, da AlmapBBDO, lança a linha Sempre Nova, com uma série de modelos para mulheres, crianças e bebês. Testado com o nosso Test Your Ad, o comercial atinge um alto score de 4,3 Estrelas, contra 2,7 da média da TV brasileira colocando o filme entre os 10% melhores anúncios do país e com uma Fluência acima da média onde 89% das pessoas reconhecem a marca.

Humor e Surpresa

Esse ano em Cannes Adam Morgan (eatbigfish) e Jon Evans (Uncensored CMO), com dados da System1 e contribuições de Peter Field, Karen Nelson-Field e Orlando Wood, defenderam que a Surpresa é uma das ferramentas estratégicas mais poderosas que existem, e quase ninguém a trata assim.

O que acontece no cérebro: A surpresa amplifica a emoção em cerca de 400%, e dura apenas uma fração de segundo (algo como 1/125 de segundo). Nessa fração, ela concentra a atenção e depois a imprime na memória. A mecânica é simples: o cérebro só presta atenção ao que não previu.

Surpresa que muda comportamento escolhe uma crença e a desmonta. A crença limitante de Ipanema poderia ser: sandália é tudo igual, e usar a mesma que todo mundo usa é o normal. Ipanema desafia o padrão com uma frase cultural familiar, que gera interesse e até uma certa tensão, mas como um plot twist. No teste vemos que os 21% de Surpresa e todos os verbatins de caráter positivo capturam a atenção para dar vazão à Felicidade, ao humor, a ironia.

E humor tem mecânicas. Uma delas é a quebra de previsão. O cérebro adivinha o que vem a seguir. Quando a virada, a surpresa chega, ele sai do piloto automático e entra num estado mais intenso e prazeroso.

Outra é a sustentação de duas verdades ao mesmo tempo. A frase continua sendo a bronca que todo mundo conhece e, simultaneamente, vira uma provocação ao adulto. Esse tipo de leitura dupla é território do hemisfério direito do cérebro, e que uma comunicação puramente literal não consegue entregar.

A terceira é deixar o público completar a piada. Reconhecer a situação, ler os personagens e perceber a virada faz parte da graça. Quem assiste não está recebendo uma mensagem, está participando dela. No teste vemos esses registros na jornada emocional, onde é possível capturar o momento em que o público reage surpreso à inversão de papéis e duplo sentido e também dando um zoom no dos Tipos de Felicidade com a predominância de “Divertido”.

E surpresa não é uma coisa só. Tem o “oh” curto e o “ohhh” longo

O “oh” curto é o inesperado narrativo. O benefício é atenção e memorabilidade, e a memória fica presa à execução.

O “ohhh” longo muda a relação da pessoa com a marca ou com a categoria. O benefício é uma mudança de atitude no longo prazo:

O filme da Ipanema parece ter os dois. A criança dizendo a frase é um “oh” curto: ninguém esperava ouvir aquilo de uma criança. A pergunta que vem junto, por que você usa o mesmo que todo mundo?, tenta o “ohhh” longo, porque mexe na relação da pessoa com o status-quo. Essa é uma das muitas leituras possíveis, mas se esse “ohhh” longo se realiza, só a o tempo e a consistência podem dizer.

E formos falar de ironia, seria a de orçamento. O publicitário Greg Hahn resumiu assim: você não tem verba para ser chato. Quem tenta ser lembrado com pouco precisa de mais surpresa, não de menos.

"Num mercado com tantas opções, acreditamos que o papel da Ipanema vai além do produto: é incentivar a autenticidade e acompanhar as diferentes formas de expressão das consumidoras brasileiras — algo que só é verdade porque a marca constrói, há anos, um portfólio amplo e diverso de produtos.

“Você não é todo mundo” traduz exatamente isso — o reconhecimento de que não existe um único jeito de ser, vestir ou viver. A campanha materializa essa mensagem de um jeito proprietário, criativo, com o toque certo de atrevimento.

É um insight cultural potente e verdadeiro, que entrega justamente o que buscávamos para este novo momento: distinção, ousadia e emoção. “Você não é todo mundo” marca essa virada para a Ipanema e é o ponto de partida para tudo o que vem a seguir."

Daiane Fischer, Gerente de Marca e Comunicação Ipanema

"Quando olhamos para o desempenho junto ao público core, vemos resultados muito fortes nas três métricas, um feito especialmente importante para uma marca que retorna com um novo posicionamento, uma nova linguagem e desafiando as convenções da categoria.

É uma demonstração de que, quando uma marca encontra uma conexão genuína entre seus diferenciais, o comportamento das pessoas e a capacidade de ressignificar códigos, ela não apenas chama atenção: gera emoção, constrói memorabilidade e conquista um espaço próprio. É esse diferencial que queremos fortalecer cada vez mais para Ipanema dentro da categoria."

João Fernandes, CSO AlmapBBDO

entry.content:
Renata Buess
Creative & Media Partnership Director, LATAM (renata.buess@system1research.com)

Published: 15 October 2026

It Takes More Than Cuteness to Reach 4.3 Stars

Ipanema

You’re not everyone

4,3
View in Portuguese

“You’re not everybody”: the phrase that ends arguments now sells… sandals

There is a phrase that ends negotiations with children anywhere in the world, with no appeal and no reply. It tends to be said a second before the child realizes the conversation is over: “You’re not everybody.”

Now imagine that phrase coming from a child. In Ipanema’s new film, it is the little ones who say it. And it is the adults who get the ticking-off.

The ad, from AlmapBBDO, launches the Sempre Nova range, with a series of styles for women, children, and babies. Tested with our Test Your Ad, the ad achieves a high score of 4.3 Stars, against a Brazilian TV average of 2.7. That puts the film among the top 10% of ads in the country, with above-average Fluency: 89% of people recognize the brand.

Humor and Surprise

This year in Cannes, Adam Morgan (eatbigfish) and Jon Evans (Uncensored CMO), with data from System1 and contributions from Peter Field, Karen Nelson-Field, and Orlando Wood, argued that Surprise is one of the most powerful strategic tools there is, and that almost nobody treats it that way.

What happens in the brain: Surprise amplifies emotion by around 400% and lasts only a fraction of a second (something like 1/125 of a second). In that instant, it focuses attention and then imprints the moment on memory. The mechanism is simple: the brain only pays attention to what it did not predict.

Surprise that changes behavior picks a belief and dismantles it. Ipanema’s limiting belief could be: sandals are all the same, and wearing what everyone else wears is normal. Ipanema challenges the norm with a familiar cultural phrase that creates interest and even a certain tension, much like a plot twist. In the test, we can see that the 21% Surprise, together with all the positive verbatims, captures attention and makes room for Happiness, humor, and irony.

And humor has mechanics. One of them is the break in prediction. The brain guesses what comes next. When the twist arrives and the surprise lands, it leaves autopilot and enters a more intense, more pleasurable state.

Another is holding two truths at the same time. The phrase remains the telling-off everyone knows and, at the same time, becomes a provocation aimed at the adult. This kind of double reading is the territory of the brain’s right hemisphere, and purely literal communication cannot deliver it.

The third is letting the audience complete the joke. Recognizing the situation, reading the characters, and spotting the twist is part of the fun. Viewers are not receiving a message; they are taking part in it. In the test, we see this in the emotional journey, where it is possible to capture the moment the audience reacts with surprise to the role reversal and the double meaning, and, zooming in on Happiness Types, a predominance of “Amused.”

But Surprise is not one thing only. There is the short “oh” and the long “ohhh.”

The short “oh” is the narrative unexpected. The benefit is attention and memorability, and the memory stays tied to the execution.

The long “ohhh” changes the person’s relationship with the brand or the category. The benefit is a shift in attitude over the long term.

Ipanema’s film seems to have both. The child saying the phrase is a short “oh”: nobody expected to hear that from a child. The question that comes with it, “why do you wear the same as everyone else?”, reaches for the long “ohhh,” because it challenges the person’s relationship with the status quo. That is one of many possible readings, and whether this long “ohhh” is fulfilled, only time and consistency can tell.

And if we are talking about irony, there is one about budgets. The adman Greg Hahn put it this way: you don’t have the budget to be boring. Anyone trying to be remembered on a small budget needs more surprise, not less.

"In a market with so many options, we believe Ipanema’s role goes beyond the product: it is to encourage authenticity and to keep pace with the many ways Brazilian women express themselves. That is only true because the brand has spent years building a broad and diverse product portfolio.

“Você não é todo mundo” (“You’re not everybody”) captures exactly that: the recognition that there is no single way to be, to dress, or to live. The campaign brings this message to life in a way that is ownable and creative, with just the right touch of daring.

It is a powerful and genuine cultural insight, and it delivers exactly what we were looking for in this new moment: distinctiveness, boldness, and emotion. “Você não é todo mundo” marks this turning point for Ipanema and is the starting point for everything that comes next."

Daiane Fischer, Brand and Communications Manager Ipanema

"When we look at performance among the core audience, we see very strong results across all three metrics — an especially significant achievement for a brand relaunching with a new positioning, a new language, and challenging category conventions.

It shows that when a brand finds a genuine connection between its differentiators, people’s behavior, and the ability to reshape codes, it doesn’t just capture attention: it generates emotion, builds memorability, and earns a space of its own. This is the differentiator we want to keep strengthening for Ipanema within the category."

João Fernandes, CSO AlmapBBDO

When Jersey Mike’s signed up Danny DeVito as their first celebrity endorser in 2023, the potential was clear. DeVito has a deserved reputation as an actor who always brings his best to ads, delighting audiences with guest spots for brands like M&Ms and Nespresso. The sandwich restaurant was hiring a proven winner.

What people might not have predicted, though, is how successful the brand would be in using DeVito in synergy with another partnership, with the NFL. That sponsorship is entering its second year and the brand alongside agency Highdive have teamed DeVito up with Eli Manning in a combination that’s delivering surreal humour and great ads.

The concept – established with the 2025 football season ads – is that DeVito and Eli Manning have an unlikely rivalry. This year’s ad, “Stacked And Jacked”, sees DeVito become an extremely unlikely football star after his years of lifting Jersey Mike’s enormous stacked subs have given him a “golden arm”. A scout spots his incredible throw and a dazzling rise to stardom follows, with poor Eli Manning having to start his own sub lifting training to catch up.

It’s a silly, surreal and delightfully enjoyable ad which uses both its celebrity guests to excellent effect. At System1 we’ve learned that the key to using celebrities well is to magnify their public persona, and at the same time give the audience the excitement of seeing them in circumstances you never normally would.

So DeVito gets to act the loveable schlub he’s been playing so well for years, and his comedy means Eli Manning just has to act as his baffled foil. We get the amusement of seeing an unlikely triumph and the schadenfreude of watching a legend of the game in second place – even if it’s all a fantasy, those are still effective emotional levers for the audience.

The result is an ad that’s very strong in our Test Your Ad measures of creative effectiveness. “Stacked And Jacked” hits a 4.5-Star Rating, which puts it in the top 13% of its category. Fast Food and Coffee Shop ads tend to be good but not exceptional, clustering in the 3-Star range, so Jersey Mike’s is leveraging its celebrities well here to easily beat the norm. The ad also scores an Exceptional rating on our short-term Spike measure which predicts immediate sales boosts.

What an individual test can’t measure is the value of creative consistency, which our reports and studies – like Compound Creativity – show becomes more valuable over time. The longer you stick with a creative idea, be it a spokesperson, a brand platform, or a continued narrative like the DeVito/Manning rivalry, the more business impact it will have. As the Jersey Mike’s/NFL partnership hits its second year, the brand is producing ads which are extremely well set to make that impact a reality.

We live in an era of collaboration. Mergers, mash-ups and multiverses sit at the heart of media, influencers and content creators love to excite fans with collabs, and naturally this all extends to our shopping baskets. A lot of the most popular innovations are brand collaborations, and a savvy modern marketer is always on the lookout for the right ones.

Brand collabs are an area where Test Your Innovation can excel. It will spot a great idea, like this week’s Innovation Of The Week, Cadbury’s Delights combination with Oreo cookies. But it’s also an excellent way to quickly pick up on collaborations that don’t make sense to consumers at a basic level, by being emotionally neutral, too difficult to grasp, or just not feeling like a great idea. The Test Your Innovation combo of personal response and market-oriented share-buying leaves nowhere to hide for collabs that don’t come off.

Fortunately, this week we’re talking about a collaboration that really does work. Cadbury Delights x Oreo scored an exceptional 5.3-Stars on Test Your Innovation, our core measure that predicts the in-market success of new products. It’s a permanent addition to Cadbury’s successful lower-calorie Delights range, which markets itself as little treats that don’t skimp on indulgence or taste. The two Mondelez brands feel like a natural fit, with Cadbury’s core platform of everyday joy a great match for Oreo’s emphasis on playfulness.

There’s deeper insight into that playfulness, and Oreo’s approach to innovation in general, in an Uncensored CMO episode where Jon Evans and Oreo CMO Eugenia Zalis chat about Oreo’s love of collaborations and how the cookie brand approaches them. Oreo has a great reputation for collabs among marketers and shoppers alike, with team-ups across categories and even media: Zalis talks about a Coca-Cola collaboration and one with superstar Post Malone.

The brand knows its fans want to have fun and picks out collaborations with that in mind, making the distinction between ‘core’ and ‘extension’ more fluid. The strategic value of a collaboration might simply be in how much the brand’s fans love it!

The Cadbury Delights bar is a permanent range addition, not a seasonal novelty, but fun is still at the heart of the product offer – customers see Oreo as adding to the idea of low-calorie high-flavour indulgence, with a 55% “Happiness” emotional response way above the 36% country average.

Stepping away from emotion to the other elements that make up the Test Your Innovation Star Rating, the bars are also seen as an objectively good bet – a strong 72% say they would buy shares in it, making the decision exceptionally quickly. And in the “implicit attributes” section, the Cadbury bars score particularly well on “brand fit”, “distinctive” and “trustworthy”, which is all further proof that this collaboration is a natural one for both brands.

Collaborations have their risks, especially when it’s two established brands. You’re exciting the fans of both, potentially expanding your market, but also risk annoying fans of your brand who dislike the other. That’s part of the reason you test the idea. But while no collab is perfect, this one is a great example of a 5-Star synergy that gets the balance between playfulness and satisfaction just right.

entry.content:

Less is More in Outdoor: The Design Rule for Ads that Actually Stand Out

For outdoor and DOOH, visuals are everything. One image. A fleeting chance to capture attention. Just 2 seconds to land brand recognition, emotion, impact.

Lots of brands doing it wrong.

In outdoor advertising, it’s easy for brands to assume that the louder they shout, the more attention they’ll get. In reality, adding more messaging, product shots or visual stimuli won’t actually drive more attention, and instead, brands risk overcrowding their poster or billboard with a jumble of visuals that don’t make sense together. Instead of standing out, their branding blends into chaos and cognitive overload.

So how can brands use tried and tested techniques to sharpen up their visuals and draw attention to their branding? System1’s expert consultants, Guillaume Garnier and Hannah Parry dug into our Test Your Ad database to find out.

Enter The 60/30/10 Rule.

The 60/30/10 rule is a well-established guideline in interior and web design to create visually appealing colour schemes, by using a combination of 3 colours in a specific way.

60% of the design should be a dominant colour; the main colour covering most of the space.

30% of the design should be a secondary colour; one that complements the dominant colour and frames the colour palette.

The last 10% should be an accent colour; a contrasting colour that gets used sparingly to add interest.

The great thing about this rule is the use of the accent colour. Keeping contrasting colours to only 10% of the design means they can be utilised to draw the eye to certain details, which allows specific elements of branding and messaging to be highlighted without being outshone.

And we’ve got the data to prove it!

Outdoor Brand Recognition: Street Smart Colours.

This is already a well-known rule of aesthetics for interior and web designers, but creatives can apply the same principles to outdoor advertising, to ensure the eye is drawn to the right places. If an outdoor ad uses an accent colour to highlight brand colours, logos, distinctive assets or product, this will enable quicker brand recognition, as the viewer is naturally drawn to looking at those details.

Jaffa Cakes’ Sweet Approach to Colour.

Take this ad from Jaffa Cakes and TBWA\London by example. The white accent colour immediately draws the eye to the brand name, and the secondary colour also stands out easily against the blue background.  All three colours signal to Jaffa Cakes’ branding, and the distinctive assets are easily recognisable. This is reflected in the ad’s exceptional Fast Fluency score of 88%, which is 28% higher than the average Fast Fluency on System1’s database of UK outdoor.

Fast Fluency is System1’s measure of how quickly an audience can identify which brand the ad they are viewing is for.  Fast Fluency mimics real life viewing scenario’s giving respondents just 2 seconds to name the brand, simulating the 2 second viewing window a passerby may have with outdoor ads in real life. So, if the visuals purposefully draw attention to branding, the viewer should be more likely to identify the brand, quickly. With such a short window, brands can’t afford to leave recognition to chance, which is exactly why techniques like the 60/30/10 rule are so valuable.

Contrast Carries.

However, not all brands have the luxury of a distinctive colour palette like Jaffa Cakes, but that’s no reason to miss out. Colours can still lean into high contrast pairings to allow other distinctive assets such as character, typeface or even pack shapes to pop.

For example, Ralph Lauren turned its iconic pony logo pink for a Cancer awareness campaign. This doesn’t relate to the usual colours of the brand, but the use of a bold black background immediately pulls the eye to the recognisable logo. With an exceptional Fast Fluency score of 82, Ralph Lauren proves that even without a signature palette, the colour contrast can still make branding land.

Heinz’s Saucy Colour Palette.

 

Similarly, Heinz use a limited but intentional colour palette in this outdoor ad, which resulted in an exceptional fast fluency score of 90%. The recognisable Heinz logo and product itself are being made to stand out here, ensuring that viewers don’t miss the branding in this ad.

The accent colour draws the viewer first to the Heinz label and then lets them take in the context within the ad: that Heinz is so good, it can be used to bait people into a mouse trap, just as the colours have baited our attention here.

The Verdict: Three’s A Crowd-Pleaser.

The 60/30/10 rule makes sense in advertising because, when visuals create a sense of balance, the eye can move comfortably from one focal point to the next.

Jaffa Cakes, Heinz, and Ralph Lauren prove the point: a disciplined palette and a well-placed accent colour send Fast Fluency soaring. It makes it easier for viewers to take in the key message being conveyed, and it’s an opportunity to match the colour palette of the brand with the colour palette of the ad.

Importantly, the 60/30/10 rule is not just about using three colours but using them strategically. If you aren’t using these colour proportions to highlight your branding or key message, you’re missing out on vital Fast Fluency points, as viewers see the ad but miss the message.

Create with Confidence®

At System1, we help brands maximise real-world commercial impact at every stage of the creative process. Our expert consultants team can help you refine and sharpen any ad, idea or concept at any stage of the development process, even down to details such as colour ration. And with metrics to mimic real life behaviour and viewing scenarios, Test Your Ad allows you to benchmark exactly how quickly your brand springs to mind, so your next outdoor ad can stand out where it counts.

The Hit Return of Mars’ Unexpected Guests

Snickers

Unexpected Guests

5.3

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market.

Request a Demo of Test Your Innovation

The last few years have seen Halloween become an advertising battleground, with Spooky Season themes and promotions ever-present on social media and traditional channels. The heart of the holiday remains candy, though, and Mars’ M&Ms brand have a tradition of silly, scary, and funny Halloween ads.

That also means they’ve got a successful back catalogue of ads ready to show again. Wear-out is a myth, and seasonal perennial ads (like the Hershey Kisses and Coca-Cola Trucks at Christmas) are a budget-friendly source of reliable effectiveness. If you’re a brand with high quality seasonal ad inventory, it’s never a mistake to re-use the best ones.

In 2024 M&Ms made a very special appearance in a Halloween ad, a collaboration with Snickers which acts as a double promotion for Halloween candy. The M&Ms spokescandies have gone trick or treating in costume themselves, to the confusion of the humans they visit who are handing out treat-size Snickers. The man points out that as giant candies the animated creatures may have more to fear at Halloween than most. The M&Ms make themselves scarce, Snickers in hand.

Officially “Unexpected Guests”, by BBDO, is a Snickers commercial, but of course it’s doing double duty as an M&Ms one too, and both brands are prominent. Which means both brands reap the benefits of its effectiveness, as the ad is back on screen this Spooky Season for a second go.

And it’s not lost any of its power to entertain. “Unexpected Guests” scores an exceptional 5.3-Stars, which puts it in the top 8% of all US candy ads. Candy is a popular and highly emotional category – at 3.7-Stars it has one of our highest norms in Test Your Ad. That means it’s even more important to make ads which entertain, delight and stand out from the crowd like this does.

The high scores and continued effectiveness of this ad raises the question of why there is such a turnover of new candy commercials every year. Given it’s a very tough category to truly excel in, why don’t more companies do what Mars is doing here and continue to run with the best ads they already have?

Sure, this is playing devil’s advocate a little – if you have campaigns as reliable, consistent and good as Snickers and M&Ms have had over the years, especially with the M&M spokescandies, why wouldn’t you make new ads? But we’ve long pointed out that chasing novelty over consistency is a high-risk, high-expense strategy for brands which is proven to not be as effective over time as investing in great work and great characters.

There’s no good reason for Mars not to run “Unexpected Guests” every year, since it’s an unusual and seasonal ad that boosts two brands with one spot. Halloween may be the time for unexpected guests, but it’s familiar presences that move the effectiveness needle.

What does a 5-Star idea look like? This week’s Innovation Of The Week is one of the top-scoring ideas in our database, a chocolate treat from Hershey’s with a premium twist. Hershey’s Creme Bars are chocolate bars with flavored creme fillings, available both as bars and in bags of individual pieces. They launched last month with two flavors – Affogato, a coffee creme variety, and Salted Caramel.

A major new Hershey’s launch is always big news and a candy brand this big isn’t likely to leave much to chance. The brand recruited pop girl group KATSEYE for a launch campaign stressing the themes of individual expression and trying something new. But what we can report is that the Creme Bars look like as safe a bet as you can get in product innovation – a true 5-Star idea that we predict to perform exceptionally well.

In our Test Your Innovation report Hershey’s Creme Bars score 5.8-Stars, only a point off the maximum rating. The Star Rating reflects the level of positive emotional response the idea received, how many consumers would “buy” (or sell) shares in the product, and the speed at which they make that decision. Emotional pull alone achieved a terrific 60% happiness score vs the US average of 38%. The responses show that while the “yummy” looking product and especially the caramel flavor are driving happiness there’s a lot of positivity simply around the Hershey’s brand – “all-time favorite” says one popular comment. It shows how years of goodwill around a brand’s core offering prepare the ground for new product lines.

Of course new products can’t just coast on their parent brand’s reputation – they have to be appealing in their own right. Hershey’s Creme Bars also perform brilliantly on the “share trading” part of Test Your Innovation, where we reflect predicted market sentiment by asking people if they’d buy shares in the new product. An exceptional 77% would.

The new product is also very Fluent – easy for consumers to understand. We get our Fluency metric by passively measuring the time taken to decide on share buying, which acts as a proxy for how quickly and decisively they ‘get’ the idea. Candy is an area where decision times are high – people grasp new concepts fast – but even so Hershey’s excelled here.

The diagnostic reports show that if there’s one area a minority of the audience is slightly wary about, it’s the texture of the creme – something only trying the product can resolve. But the implicit attributes – levels of rapid association with the new idea – show scores well above the average for “Premium”, “High-Quality” and “Recommended”, predicting that the Creme Bars will find a place as a slightly different and more sophisticated product within the Hershey’s range.

Birra Moretti and Stanley Tucci Flip the Beer Ad Script

Birra Moretti

Too Busy Enjoying Life

4.3

Make creative your competitive edge; unlock insights and inspiration from 100,000+ ads, rooted in emotional response, to predict and improve your creative’s business impact. Access every Ad Of The Week in our Topical Ads categories.

Request a Demo of Test Your Ad Competitive Edge

Lucky Generals’ latest ad for Italian beer brand Birra Moretti delights in deconstructing beer ad conventions. They’ve created a clever meta-commercial that still achieves close alignment between its star, actor Stanley Tucci, and the brand and its values.

The ad inverts expectations. All the typical elements of a premium beer ad are here – a beautiful landscape, an artfully arranged product, a celebrity brand ambassador and friends enjoying a social occasion. But they’re not all in the same place. The conceit of Birra Moretti’s ad is that Stanley Tucci is meant to be starring in it, and the set dressers are preparing the perfect beer shot for him, but he’s not shown up. Why not? Because he’s enjoying great food, great company and a Birra Moretti of his own, of course, and he’s sent a video message instead.

Of course everything is scripted, but even so splitting the ad between the artifice of a typical beer ad and Tucci’s more spontaneous and joyful vertical video creates a real contrast. It positions Tucci – and the brand – on the side of authenticity, socialising and cheerful chaos.

And by adopting the vertical video format that’s so embedded in the way young consumers communicate, it’s also putting the brand on the side of youth. And the Test Your Ad demographic results indicate that the ad is resonating especially well with a younger audience.

That’s not the only piece of good news for Birra Moretti in the results. Their ad scores a 4.3-Star Rating in a category where the average is 3.1-Stars. Beer and cider ads are an unusual case where the category norm is slightly above average for all ads but very few commercials really stand out. Most are just…OK. Birra Moretti aims higher and gets there, it’s in the top 10% of all UK beer and cider ads we’ve tested.

What makes it work isn’t just the clever set-up wrong-footing the viewer. It’s the natural bonhomie of Stanley Tucci himself, proving why his laid back good humour is such an asset for the brand. In a sector where premium Italian beers can sometimes act a little pretentious, Birra Moretti is all about quality, but in the context of good times and simple pleasures. Stanley Tucci and his performance in this ad aligns perfectly with that. It’s a great example of a celebrity brand ambassador being used creatively and fitting exactly with the image and mood the brand wants to own. This ad takes a big step in that direction.

Cheez-Its Have Fun With College Football

Cheez-Its

9th Year Seniors

4.1

Want to stay ahead of the latest winning innovation trends? Innovation of the Week, powered by System1’s Test Your Innovation testing, is your regular spotlight on the newest concepts hitting the market.

Request a Demo of Test Your Innovation

With the college football season starting, Cheez-Its’ cheeky new ad takes a provocative look at a question that’s on a lot of fans’ minds right now – how old is too old to play college football? Players at college level are trending older, and in 2024 one athlete qualified for a record-breaking ninth time. That’s the inspiration for Cheez-Its “9th Year Seniors” ad – and they really do mean senior, with an octogenarian player ready to kick some ass on the field.

The ad is part of Cheez-Its’ ongoing campaign with BBDO New York, the “College Couch Committee”, a group of fans pronouncing on matters of football from the couch, with Cheez-Its to hand. An animated Cheez-It mascot also takes part, pointing out that aging only makes the players “cheesier, saltier and yummier”. The verdict: let the old guy play.

Cheez-Its pack a lot into a short space here, with not one of the spot’s 16 seconds wasted. It’s a confident, quick-fire and very funny ad that also works as a conversation starter about an issue football fans have plenty of opinions about. Taking a tongue-in-cheek stand on a subject like 9th-year seniors positions Cheez-Its as a brand that understands fan culture, and can have some fun with it too.

The “Committee” angle structures the ad and also allows for plenty of dialogue and non verbal interplay, important sources of the connection and ‘between-ness’ that creates emotional impact in an ad. The Committee is an example of a ‘Scenario’ Fluent Device – a repeating narrative construct that drives the creative in an ad. Like the more common ‘Character’ Fluent Device this works by creating consistency that builds familiarity and creates an expectation of entertainment.

Our Test Your Ad report shows the result of this approach – the ad is a huge success, and with a general audience, not even just among football fans. The ad gets Exceptional scores for both short-term Spike Rating and fast recognition Brand Fluency, and a long-term Star Rating than puts it in the top 11% of all US savory snack ads.

These are excellent scores for a 15-second ad that’s tied to a specific tournament – what could have shown niche appeal in fact has general effectiveness for Cheez-Its. Strong branding from the beginning and a punchline viewers who haven’t followed the specific 9th year senior story can understand make the ad a success, and show that being funny and having a point of view are usually strong commercial plays.
